summary: A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array that satisfies the heap property: in a min-heap every parent is less than or equal to its children, so the minimum is always at the root. It is the standard implementation of a priority queue.

sections.heading: Structure
bullets: Complete binary tree: every level is full except possibly the last, filled left to right.
Stored in an array with no pointers.
Min-heap: parent <= children. Max-heap: parent >= children.
Not fully sorted: siblings have no ordering.

sections.heading: Insert (sift up)
sections.body: Append at the end, then swap with the parent while the new value is smaller. O(log n).

sections.heading: Extract-min (sift down)
sections.body: Take the root, move the last element to the root, then swap it with the smaller child until the property holds. O(log n).

sections.heading: Complexity
bullets: build-heap from n items: O(n) by sifting down from the last parent.
Heap sort: O(n log n), in place, not stable.

subtopics.title: Why build-heap is O(n)
subtopics.summary: Most nodes are near the bottom.

sections.body: Half the nodes are leaves needing no work, a quarter move at most one level, and so on. The sum n/2·0 + n/4·1 + n/8·2 + ... converges to O(n), better than n inserts at O(n log n).

Build a max-heap, then repeatedly swap the root with the last element and sift down on a shrinking heap. O(n log n) worst case and O(1) space, but poor cache behaviour makes it slower than quick sort in practice.

bullets: K largest/smallest elements with a size-k heap.
Median of a stream with a max-heap and a min-heap.

subtopics.title: Heap memory vs heap data structure

sections.body: The process heap used by malloc has nothing to do with this tree-shaped structure beyond the shared name.

takeaways: Complete binary tree in an array; root is the min (or max).
Insert and extract are O(log n); peek is O(1); build-heap is O(n).
Basis of priority queues and heap sort.
